answer: In the multilingual tweet annotation study, about 15% of tweets were intentionally duplicated to be annotated twice—either by the same annotator or by two different annotators—so that self-agreement (from repeated annotations by the same annotator) and inter-annotator agreement (from annotations by different annotators) could be computed; this addressed annotator quality and the objective difficulty of the task, with inter-annotator agreement approximating an upper bound on classifier performance [1]. For classifier evaluation, the labeled set was partitioned into 10 folds, with one fold held out for testing and the remaining nine used for training, repeated until each fold was tested once, and confidence intervals were estimated from the standard deviations across the 10 tests; blocked, stratified 10-fold cross-validation was applied in all experiments [1]. In the time-ordered Twitter sentiment evaluation, 138 in-sample/out-of-sample dataset pairs were created by language and time window, where each out-set always follows its in-set and consists of the subsequent 10,000 consecutive tweets (or the remainder), serving as the gold standard; the in-sets were used to compare six estimation procedures—three cross-validation variants (stratified blocked, non-stratified blocked, stratified random) and three sequential validation variants (9:1 with 20 equidistant samples, 9:1 with 10 equidistant samples, 2:1 with 10 semi-equidistant samples)—to assess how well in-sample estimates approximate out-of-sample performance, addressing the uncertainty from temporal ordering and data dependence [2]. The study found that cross-validation variants tend to overestimate performance while sequential methods tend to underestimate it, and that standard random cross-validation is significantly worse than blocked cross-validation and should not be used for time-ordered data [2].
